title: Subsets
description:
# Subsets

Given an integer array `nums` whose elements are all **unique**, return all possible subsets, also called the power set.

A subset may contain zero or more elements from `nums`. Each input index can be used at most once. Because every value in `nums` is unique, the answer must contain exactly `2^nums.length` distinct subsets.

Both the subsets and the elements within each subset may appear in any order. Include the empty subset `[]`.

## Example 1

**Input**
nums = [1,2,3]

**Output**
[[],[1],[2],[1,2],[3],[1,3],[2,3],[1,2,3]]

## Example 2

**Input**
nums = [0]

**Output**
[[],[0]]

## Constraints

* `1 <= nums.length <= 10`
* `-10 <= nums[i] <= 10`
* All values in `nums` are unique.

## Follow-up

Can you explain why every correct algorithm must produce `2^n` subsets before accounting for the cost of copying elements into the answer?

solutions.name: Backtracking with Growing Start Index
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat the current path as a valid subset at every recursion node, append a copy of it to the answer, and then try every later value as the next chosen element. After returning from recursion, remove that value so the next branch starts from the previous path.

## Key Insight

The `start` index is the invariant that prevents reusing an element or generating the same subset through a different order. Recording each intermediate path is correct because subsets have no fixed target length.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n * 2^n), because there are `2^n` subsets and copying each subset can cost up to `n`.
- Space Complexity: O(n) for the recursion path, excluding the returned answer.

solutions.name: Include-or-Skip Recursion
solutions.description:
## Approach

Process positions from left to right. At each index, first recurse without the current value, then add the value and recurse again. When the index reaches the end of the array, copy the current path into the answer.

## Key Insight

Every element has exactly two states: excluded or included. This forms a binary decision tree with `2^n` leaves, which is the direct definition of the power set.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n * 2^n), because each leaf copies a subset.
- Space Complexity: O(n) for the recursion stack and path, excluding the returned answer.

solutions.name: Bit Mask Enumeration
solutions.description:
## Approach

Loop through every integer mask from `0` to `2^n - 1`. Bit `i` of the mask says whether `nums[i]` belongs to the current subset. Build one subset per mask and append it to the answer.

## Key Insight

A subset is a binary choice vector. Integer masks encode that vector compactly and make the exact count of subsets visible in the loop bounds.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n * 2^n), because each mask checks `n` bits.
- Space Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space beyond the subset currently being copied and the returned answer.

solutions.name: Iterative Cascading
solutions.description:
## Approach

Start with only the empty subset. For each value in `nums`, take a snapshot of the subsets already present, copy each one, append the new value to the copy, and add the copy to the answer.

## Key Insight

Each new value doubles the number of known subsets: every old subset has one version without the value and one version with it. This route makes the output growth easy to see without recursion.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n * 2^n), because every generated subset may be copied as it grows.
- Space Complexity: O(n * 2^n) for the returned answer.

tests.description: Canonical three-value example produces eight subsets.
Single zero verifies the empty subset and singleton subset are both present.
Negative, zero, and positive values must be preserved.
Constraint boundary values are valid subset elements.
Input does not need to be sorted; subset membership matters, not global ordering.
Four values produce sixteen subsets and expose exponential growth.
Four mixed-sign values verify larger output with negative numbers.
Unsorted boundary and zero values verify no hidden sorting assumption.
A simple positive triple catches implementations that omit size-two subsets.
Descending input checks that all positions are considered independently.
Another mixed set broadens value coverage without changing subset semantics.
